Autoregressive Nets, Moment Matching & GSNs

Three more ways to teach a network to dream, and how to tell which one dreams best

GANs, VAEs and diffusion models are not the only way to generate data. An autoregressive network writes an image one pixel at a time, each pixel a coin flip whose odds depend on everything already drawn, and in exchange it tells you the exact probability of any image. A moment-matching network trains a generator with no critic at all, just a kernel that compares two clouds of points. And a denoising autoencoder, run in a loop of “add noise, clean up”, turns into a Markov chain that wanders among plausible images. In the figure, two models trained on real handwritten digits are generating as you watch: NADE pixel by pixel, and a denoising chain a whole image per step. Touch either panel to start a new sample.

Directed generative nets

Sigmoid belief nets: hidden causes, sampled top-down

A directed generative net describes how data is made: start at the top, draw the hidden variables, then draw each layer given the one above, all the way down to the pixels. That recipe is called ancestral sampling, and it is always easy. The VAE generator and the GAN generator of the last two chapters are directed nets with continuous hidden variables and a deterministic map to the data. The oldest member of the family keeps everything binary: the sigmoid belief network (Neal, 1992). Every unit is a coin that comes up 1 with probability σ(weighted sum of its parents + bias). With enough hidden units in enough layers, such a net can represent any distribution over binary vectors (Sutskever & Hinton, 2008).

Sampling is easy; the reverse question is not. Given an image, which causes produced it? Two causes that are independent before you look become rivals once you see their common effect: if a pixel is on and you learn that its row bar is on, the column bar is no longer needed to explain it. This is explaining away, and it is why the posterior over hidden units does not factorise and why exact inference must, in general, sum over every hidden configuration. Below is a tiny belief net with eight hidden causes, one per row bar and one per column bar of a 4 × 4 image, small enough to sum all 28 = 256 configurations exactly. Click pixels to switch them on, and watch the posterior over the bars.

\[ \begin{aligned} p(h_j = 1) &= \sigma(a) \\ p(v_i = 1 \mid \mathbf h) &= \sigma\Big(\sum_j W_{ij} h_j + b_i\Big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: each of the eight bars hj is switched on independently with prior probability σ(a). A pixel vi then turns on with a probability that rises with the total weight Wij of the bars that cover it. Here Wij = w if bar j covers pixel i (else 0) and bi = −w/2, so an uncovered pixel is rarely on and a covered one usually is. σ(t) = 1/(1 + e−t).
Say it“Each bar is on with probability sigma of a; each pixel is on with probability sigma of the weighted sum of the bars covering it, plus its bias.”
\[ \begin{aligned} p(\mathbf v) &= \sum_{\mathbf h \in \{0,1\}^8} p(\mathbf h)\, \prod_i p(v_i \mid \mathbf h) \\ p(\mathbf h \mid \mathbf v) &= p(\mathbf h)\,p(\mathbf v \mid \mathbf h) \,/\, p(\mathbf v) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the probability of an image adds up every way the hidden bars could have produced it, 256 terms here. Dividing one term by the total gives the posterior of that explanation. With H hidden units there are 2H terms, which is why real belief nets are trained with approximations: wake–sleep, mean-field, or a learned inference network.
Say it“p of v is the sum over all hidden settings of the prior times the likelihood; the posterior is one term over that sum.”

Auto-regressive networks

Linear auto-regressive nets: one logistic regression per pixel

Drop the hidden units altogether. The chain rule of probability says any joint distribution can be written as a product of conditionals: the first pixel, then the second given the first, then the third given the first two, and so on. An auto-regressive network models each of those conditionals with a function of the earlier pixels. Nothing is hidden, so nothing needs to be summed out: log p(x) is exact, and you can train it by maximum likelihood like any classifier. The price is the ordering (here, raster order: left to right, top to bottom) and sampling one pixel at a time.

The simplest choice makes each conditional linear. For binary pixels that means a logistic regression of pixel d on pixels 1 to d − 1: the fully visible sigmoid belief net (FVSBN; Frey, 1998). For real-valued data the same idea with linear-Gaussian conditionals gives a multivariate Gaussian. Below is an FVSBN fitted to real MNIST digits shrunk to 14 × 14 pixels: 196 separate logistic regressions, fitted by scikit-learn on 12,000 training digits and embedded in the page. Slide the pixel d to see the weights that predict it, click pixels to edit the digit, or sample a new one.

\[ \begin{aligned} p(\mathbf x) &= \prod_{d=1}^{D} p(x_d \mid x_{<d}) \\ p(x_d = 1 \mid x_{<d}) &= \sigma(\ell_d) \\ \ell_d &= b_d + \sum_{j<d} W_{dj}\, x_j \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the probability of the whole image is the product of D coin flips, each conditioned on every pixel before it. Pixel d’s coin is a logistic regression on the pixels already drawn: its logit ℓd is a bias bd plus one weight Wdj per earlier pixel. W is strictly lower-triangular, which is what makes the product a proper, normalised distribution.
Say it“p of x is the product over d of p of x-d given the earlier pixels; each is sigma of a logit, b-d plus the weighted sum of the earlier pixels.”
\[ \begin{aligned} \#\text{params} &= \tfrac{D(D-1)}{2} + D \\ \text{full table} &= 2^{D} - 1 \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: a full probability table over D binary pixels needs 2D − 1 numbers; the FVSBN needs only one weight per pair of pixels plus a bias each. For 14 × 14 = 196 pixels that is 19,306 parameters; for 28 × 28 = 784 it is 307,720, and every one is used once per image, so the cost of scoring an image grows as D2.
Say it“D times D minus one over two weights plus D biases, against two to the D, minus one, for a full table.”
p(xd = 1 | x<d)

Neural auto-regressive networks

NADE: one hidden layer, shared by every pixel

A linear conditional is too weak, and giving every pixel its own neural network (Bengio & Bengio, 2000) is expensive. The neural auto-regressive density estimator (NADE; Larochelle & Murray, 2011) finds the sweet spot by sharing weights. Every conditional uses a hidden layer hd computed from the earlier pixels with the same input weights W: pixel j always adds the same column W:,j to the hidden pre-activation, whichever later pixel is being predicted. That makes the pre-activation a running sum, so all 784 hidden layers cost about as much as one ordinary layer.

The model below has 100 hidden units, was trained in numpy on 12,000 MNIST digits for 6 passes, and is exactly the NADE of the project. Paint a digit on the left: the right panel shows, for every pixel, the probability NADE gives it of being ink given everything above and to the left, so you can watch it guess where your stroke goes next. Then let it finish the digit from any row.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf a_{d} &= \mathbf c + \textstyle\sum_{j<d} W_{:,j}\, x_j \\ \mathbf h_d &= \sigma(\mathbf a_d) \\ p(x_d = 1 \mid x_{<d}) &= \sigma\big(b_d + V_{d}\cdot \mathbf h_d\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: to predict pixel d, add up the input-weight columns of the earlier pixels that are on, squash to get a hidden vector hd of H = 100 numbers, and read pixel d’s odds off it with its own output weights Vd and bias bd. W and c are shared by all pixels; V and b are per pixel.
Say it“a-d is c plus the sum of W's columns for the earlier pixels that are on; p of x-d is sigma of b-d plus V-d dot sigma of a-d.”
\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf a_{d+1} &= \mathbf a_d + W_{:,d}\, x_d \\ \text{cost} &= O(DH) \\ \#\text{params} &= D(2H+1) + H \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: moving from pixel d to d + 1 only adds one column to the running sum, so all D conditionals cost O(DH) instead of O(D2H). With D = 784 and H = 100 the model has 157,684 parameters, about half of an FVSBN on the same images, and in Larochelle & MurrayLarochelle & Murray found it clearly more accurate than an FVSBN on every binary dataset they tried.rsquo;s experiments it was generally more accurate than an FVSBN. Training is ordinary back-propagation on the exact −log p(x).
Say it“a-d-plus-one is a-d plus column d of W times x-d; the cost is order D times H.”

Generative moment matching networks

Moment matching: train a generator with no critic

A GAN needs a second network to tell real from fake. A generative moment matching network (GMMN; Li, Swersky & Zemel, 2015; Dziugaite, Roy & Ghahramani, 2015) replaces the critic with a fixed statistic. Two distributions are the same if all their moments agree: same mean, same covariance, same third moments and so on. The maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) compares all of them at once through a kernel: it is the distance between the average feature vector of the data and the average feature vector of the generated samples. With a linear kernel it compares only means; with a quadratic kernel, means and second moments; with a Gaussian kernel, every moment, so it is zero only when the two distributions are identical. The generator, here a small network turning 2-D noise into 2-D points, is trained by back-propagating the MMD between a batch of data and a batch of its samples.

The shading is the witness function: where it is warm the data has more mass than the generator, where it is cool the generator has too much; the MMD gradient pushes samples downhill on it. Pick a kernel and press Train, then try the Gaussian with a bandwidth that is far too small or far too large.

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{MMD}^2 &= \Vert \bar\phi_{\text{data}} - \bar\phi_{\text{gen}} \Vert^2 \\ &= \tfrac{1}{m^2}\textstyle\sum_{i,i'} k(x_i,x_{i'}) \\ &\quad - \tfrac{2}{mn}\textstyle\sum_{i,j} k(x_i,y_j) \\ &\quad + \tfrac{1}{n^2}\textstyle\sum_{j,j'} k(y_j,y_{j'}) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: xi are m data points, yj = G(zj) are n generated points, and k(a, b) = φ(a)·φ(b) is a kernel. The three averages are how similar data is to data, data to samples, and samples to samples. The Gaussian kernel k(a, b) = exp(−‖a − b‖2/2σ2) has infinitely many features, which is what lets MMD see every moment. The witness function is f(u) = meani k(u, xi) − meanj k(u, yj).
Say it“MMD squared is the mean data-data kernel, minus twice the mean data-sample kernel, plus the mean sample-sample kernel.”

Drawing samples from autoencoders

Every denoising autoencoder hides a Markov chain

A denoising autoencoder learns to undo a corruption C(x̃ | x): given a damaged x̃, its decoder outputs a distribution P(x | x̃) over clean versions. Alternate the two (corrupt, then sample a clean version, then corrupt again) and you have a Markov chain. Bengio, Yao, Alain & Vincent (2013) proved the remarkable part: if P(x | x̃) is the true conditional of the data, the chain’s long-run distribution is the data distribution; if it is a consistent estimate, the long-run distribution is a consistent estimate too. So any good denoiser is secretly a generative model, and sampling from it is just running the loop. (Contractive autoencoders can be sampled in a similar way; Rifai et al., 2012.)

The lab makes this exact on a real one-dimensional distribution: how much ink (pixels on, in bins of 5) the 12,665 zeros and ones of MNIST’s training set contain. The ones are thin, the zeros heavy, so the distribution has two humps. Corruption moves a value to a uniformly random bin within r of it. The denoiser is either the exact posterior or a one-bump Gaussian fitted to that posterior’s mean and variance, the kind of simple output distribution a real network would use. Move the corruption width r and switch the denoiser; click the chart to inspect the posterior at any x̃.

\[ \begin{aligned} \tilde x_t &\sim C(\tilde x \mid x_t) \\ x_{t+1} &\sim P(x \mid \tilde x_t) \\ T(x' \mid x) &= \textstyle\sum_{\tilde x} C(\tilde x \mid x) \\ &\qquad \times P(x' \mid \tilde x) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: one step of the chain corrupts the current state and then asks the denoiser for a clean one. Summing over the hidden corrupted value gives the transition probabilities T from state x to state x′: here a 60 × 60 matrix, so the long-run distribution can be computed by repeatedly multiplying by it.
Say it“Corrupt, then denoise; T of x-prime given x is the sum over x-tilde of C of x-tilde given x times P of x-prime given x-tilde.”
\[ \begin{aligned} P(x \mid \tilde x) &\propto \pi(x)\,C(\tilde x \mid x) \\ \textstyle\sum_x \pi(x)\,T(x' \mid x) &= \pi(x') \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: if the denoiser is exactly Bayes’ rule applied to the data distribution π (prior π(x) times corruption likelihood, normalised to sum to 1 over x), then starting from π and taking one step leaves you at π: the data distribution is stationary. (Swap the sums: ∑x π(x)C(x̃ | x) is the probability of x̃, exactly the normalising constant of the posterior, so it cancels.) If the chain can reach every state, it is also the only stationary distribution.
Say it“P of x given x-tilde is proportional to pi of x times C of x-tilde given x; then pi times T equals pi.”

Clamping and conditional sampling

Clamping: sample the missing pixels, keep the rest

The chain can also answer conditional questions. Split the units into observed ones, whose values you know, and free ones. Run the same loop, but after every step clamp the observed units back to their known values, so only the free units ever change. The chain then wanders among completions that agree with what you fixed, approximately sampling P(free | observed). For images this is inpainting; for a model of (input, label) pairs it is prediction. No retraining is needed: the same denoiser does both jobs.

Here the denoiser is a real one: a tied-weight autoencoder with 200 hidden units, trained in numpy on 12,000 MNIST digits to repair images in which 30% of the pixels were replaced by random bits. The chain alternates that corruption with drawing every pixel from the decoder’s probabilities. Choose what to clamp and press Run; with nothing clamped the chain drifts from digit to digit.

\[ \begin{aligned} \tilde{\mathbf x} &\sim C\big(\tilde{\mathbf x} \mid \mathbf x_{o}, \mathbf x^{(t)}_{f}\big) \\ \mathbf x^{(t+1)}_{f} &\sim P\big(\mathbf x_{f} \mid \tilde{\mathbf x}\big) \\ \mathbf x^{(t+1)}_{o} &= \mathbf x_{o} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: o marks the observed (clamped) pixels and f the free ones. Corrupt the whole current image (salt-and-pepper: each pixel replaced by a random bit with probability q), let the denoiser propose a clean image, keep its proposal only for the free pixels, and write the observed pixels back. Run long enough, the free pixels behave like draws from their conditional distribution given the clamped ones.
Say it“Corrupt everything, resample the free pixels from the denoiser, and put the observed pixels back.”
steps
free pixels changed, last step

Walk-back training

Walk-back: train where the chain actually wanders

An ordinary denoising autoencoder only ever sees corruptions one step away from a training example. But the chain does not stay one step away: a single unlucky sample can carry it into a region the denoiser never trained on, where its output is arbitrary. There the chain may linger, putting probability on places the data never goes: spurious modes. The walk-back procedure (Bengio, Yao, Alain & Vincent, 2013) trains on the chain’s own excursions: start at a training example x0, let the current model walk a few corrupt-and-denoise steps, and at every corrupted point visited add the target “go back to x0”. It seeks out the spurious modes and pulls them down, and the authors found it speeds up training.

The lab uses the ink distribution again, but now the denoiser is learned from 300 training values: P(x | x̃) is the share of training pairs at x̃ that came from x, plus a small weight λ on “give back what you were given”, which is all an autoencoder can do where it has no training data. Raise the walk length k (k = 1 is ordinary training) and watch the chain stop getting lost at the heavy end.

\[ \begin{aligned} \tilde x_j &\sim C(\cdot \mid x_{j-1}) \\ x_j &\sim P(\cdot \mid \tilde x_j), \quad j = 1, \dots, k \\ \mathcal L &= -\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^{k} \log P\big(x_0 \mid \tilde x_j\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: walk k corruption steps away from the training value x0, using the model itself to denoise in between, and at every corrupted point x̃j train the denoiser to return the original x0. With k = 1 this is ordinary denoising training. Here “training” means counting: each pair (x̃j, x0) adds one to a table, and P(x | x̃) = (count(x̃, x) + λ[x = x̃]) / (count(x̃) + λ), which is the maximum-likelihood fit plus the copy-your-input default.
Say it“Walk k steps away from x-nought with the model's own help, and at every corrupted point, train it to come back to x-nought.”

Generative stochastic networks

Generative stochastic networks: learn the chain, not the density

A generative stochastic network (GSN; Bengio, Thibodeau-Laufer, Alain & Yosinski, 2014) takes the idea to its conclusion. Its state has a visible part x and a latent part h; each step draws a new latent state from the old latent state and the current x, then draws a new x from the latent state. The model is the transition operator; it never writes down a normalised p(x), so there is no partition function to fight, and it is trained like a walk-back autoencoder by maximising log P(x0 | hk) along the chain. The denoising autoencoder is the special case where h is just the corrupted x̃. Noise, in the pixels or injected into the latent state, is what makes the chain move.

A discriminant GSN (Zhou & Troyanskaya, 2014) runs the chain over the outputs y with the input x always clamped, so it models p(y | x) for structured outputs whose parts depend on each other; they used it to predict protein secondary structure. Predicting all the output pixels in one pass, each independently, ignores how they depend on each other; letting the chain feed its own guesses back in gives coherent strokes. Turn up the latent noise and watch the free chain travel, then switch to the structured-output task.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf h_{t} &\sim P_{\theta_1}(\mathbf h \mid \mathbf h_{t-1}, \mathbf x_{t-1}) \\ \mathbf x_{t} &\sim P_{\theta_2}(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf h_t) \\ \mathbf h_t &= \sigma\big(W^{\!\top}\tilde{\mathbf x}_{t-1} + \mathbf c + \sigma_h \boldsymbol\epsilon\big) \\ \mathbf x_t &\sim \text{Bern}\big(\sigma(W\mathbf h_t + \mathbf b)\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the general GSN step in the first two lines; in the last two, the one this page runs, built from the trained autoencoder of the last two sections. The latent state ht is the hidden layer computed from the corrupted image x̃t−1, plus Gaussian noise of size σh on its pre-activation (ε is standard normal; the autoencoder was trained with σh = 0.5). Every pixel is then drawn from the decoder. In a discriminant GSN, x is the input and stays fixed, and only the output part is resampled.
Say it“Draw the latent state from the previous state and image, then draw the image from the latent state.”

Evaluating generative models

Evaluating generative models: what a number can and cannot tell you

Comparing generative models is surprisingly treacherous. The usual yardstick is the average log-likelihood of held-out data, but it comes in three grades: exact (NADE, FVSBN), a bound (a VAE’s ELBO is a lower bound on log p, so −ELBO overstates the true cost), or a stochastic estimate (importance sampling, annealed importance sampling for Boltzmann machines). Comparing an exact number with a bound is unfair to the bounded model. The data must also be identical: a binarised digit set scored after thresholding is a different, easier task than the same digits binarised at random, and a continuous density scored on discrete pixel values can reach any likelihood it likes unless uniform noise is added first. Changing the preprocessing changes the number more than many papers’ claimed improvements.

Looking at samples is not a substitute (Theis, van den Oord & Bethge, 2016). A model that copies its training images makes perfect samples and has a terrible test likelihood. A model that produces pure noise 99% of the time can still have an excellent likelihood, because mixing in noise with weight α costs at most −log(1 − α) nats: 4.6 nats for α = 0.99. And the Parzen-window estimate once used to score GANs can be far from the truth even when the true answer is known. Here every number is computed on the same 1,000 test digits. Switch between the four things you could report and compare the samples with the score.

\[ \begin{aligned} &-\log\!\big[\alpha\,2^{-D} + (1-\alpha)\,p(\mathbf x)\big] \\ &\quad \le -\log p(\mathbf x) - \log(1-\alpha) \\ &\text{bits/pixel} = \frac{-\log p(\mathbf x)}{D \ln 2} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: a mixture that outputs uniform noise with probability α and the real model otherwise loses at most −log(1 − α) nats on every test image, however bad its samples look. Dividing nats by D ln 2 converts to bits per pixel, the unit that lets images of different sizes be compared.
Say it“Mixing in noise with weight alpha costs at most minus log of one minus alpha nats.”
\[ \hat p(\mathbf x) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^{n} \varepsilon^{\,h_i}\,(1-\varepsilon)^{D - h_i} \]
Read it as: a Parzen window (kernel density) estimate for binary images. Put a little cloud around each of n reference images si: an image at Hamming distance hi from si gets probability εhi(1 − ε)D−hi. Use 1,000 training digits as the si and it is a model that memorises; use 1,000 of NADE’s samples and it is the Parzen estimate of NADE’s likelihood.
Say it“p-hat of x is the average over reference images of epsilon to the Hamming distance times one minus epsilon to the rest.”
test −log p, nats per digit
bits per pixel

Real-world project

Project: NADE against a VAE on binarised MNIST

The data is MNIST (LeCun, Cortes & Burges): 70,000 handwritten digits of 28 × 28 grey pixels, licensed CC BY-SA 3.0 by its authors and fetched from OpenML (dataset 554). Every pixel at 128 or above becomes ink (1), the rest paper (0). Three models were trained in numpy on the same 12,000 training digits for the same 6 passes with Adam: a NADE with 100 hidden units (157,684 parameters), a VAE with a 100-unit tanh encoder and decoder and 10 latent dimensions (160,804 parameters), and, as a floor, independent pixels (784 parameters). Weights are stored as 8-bit integers with one scale per row, and the Python reference below scores exactly those stored weights. The first 1,000 MNIST test digits are embedded in this page (and shared under CC BY-SA 3.0, like the original); your browser scores all of them.

The comparison is the one the evaluation section warns about, done carefully. NADE gives an exact −log p(x). The VAE gives −ELBO, an upper bound, and the importance-weighted bound (Burda, Grosse & Salakhutdinov, 2016) with k samples, which tightens towards the true value as k grows. Score the test set, then pick a digit and slide k.

\[ \begin{aligned} \log p(\mathbf x) &\ge \mathcal L_k, \qquad \mathbf z_j \sim q(\mathbf z \mid \mathbf x) \\ \mathcal L_k &= \mathbb E\Big[\log \frac1k \sum_{j=1}^{k} w_j\Big] \\ w_j &= \frac{p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf z_j)\,p(\mathbf z_j)}{q(\mathbf z_j \mid \mathbf x)} \\ \mathcal L_1 = \text{ELBO} &\le \mathcal L_{10} \le \mathcal L_{50} \le \log p(\mathbf x) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: draw k latent codes from the encoder’s distribution q, give each an importance weight wj: how well it explains x relative to how likely q was to propose it, and average the weights before taking the log. With one sample this is the ELBO; with more samples the bound can only get tighter (in expectation). The page uses one fixed stream of 50 random draws per digit (the generator mulberry32, seeded by the digit’s index), so ℒ1, ℒ10 and ℒ50 share their draws; the ELBO row uses the KL term in closed form with the average reconstruction over the same 50 draws.
Say it“L-k is the expected log of the average importance weight over k samples; it rises from the ELBO towards log p of x.”

The same scoring in Python

import json, base64, math, numpy as np
from scipy.special import expit, logsumexp
J = json.load(open("x063-data.json"))          # the stored weights and digits this page embeds
def deq(m): q = np.frombuffer(base64.b64decode(m["q"]), np.int8).reshape(m["r"], m["c"]); return q * np.array(m["s"])[:, None]
bits = lambda s, n: np.unpackbits(np.frombuffer(base64.b64decode(s), np.uint8).reshape(n, 98), axis=1)[:, :784].astype(float)
Xte = bits(J["test"], 1000)
sp = lambda a: np.logaddexp(0, a)
def bern_nll(x, L): return (sp(L) - x * L).sum(-1)     # -log prod Bern(x; sigmoid(L))

m = np.array(J["marg"]); Lm = np.log(m / (1 - m))      # independent pixels
N = J["nade"]; W, V, b, c = deq(N["W"]), deq(N["V"]), np.array(N["b"]), np.array(N["c"])
def nade_nll(X):                                       # a_d = c + sum_{j<d} W_j x_j, all d at once
    A = c + np.concatenate([np.zeros((len(X), 1, 100)), np.cumsum(X[:, :-1, None] * W[None, :-1], axis=1)], axis=1)
    return bern_nll(X, (expit(A) * V).sum(-1) + b)

def mulberry32(a):                                     # the page's random number generator
    a &= 0xFFFFFFFF
    def r():
        nonlocal a
        a = (a + 0x6D2B79F5) & 0xFFFFFFFF; t = a
        t = ((t ^ (t >> 15)) * (1 | t)) & 0xFFFFFFFF
        t = ((t + (((t ^ (t >> 7)) * (61 | t)) & 0xFFFFFFFF)) & 0xFFFFFFFF) ^ t
        return ((t ^ (t >> 14)) & 0xFFFFFFFF) / 4294967296
    return r
def gauss(r):
    u = 0
    while u == 0: u = r()
    return math.sqrt(-2 * math.log(u)) * math.cos(2 * math.pi * r())
P = {k: (deq(v) if isinstance(v, dict) else np.array(v)) for k, v in J["vae"].items()}
def vae_part(X, K, seed0):                             # ELBO and importance-weighted bounds
    h = np.tanh(X @ P["We"] + P["be"]); mu = h @ P["Wm"] + P["bm"]; ls = h @ P["Ws"] + P["bs"]
    E = np.array([[[gauss(r) for _ in range(10)] for _ in range(K)] for r in (mulberry32(seed0 + i) for i in range(len(X)))])
    z = mu[:, None] + np.exp(ls)[:, None] * E
    L = np.tanh(z @ P["Wd"] + P["bd"]) @ P["Wo"] + P["bo"]
    lpx = -bern_nll(X[:, None], L); lw = lpx - 0.5 * (z ** 2).sum(-1) + 0.5 * (E ** 2).sum(-1) + ls.sum(-1)[:, None]
    kl = 0.5 * (mu ** 2 + np.exp(2 * ls) - 1 - 2 * ls).sum(-1)
    return lpx.mean(1) - kl, {k: logsumexp(lw[:, :k], axis=1) - math.log(k) for k in (1, 10, 50)}, kl

Wrap-up

Five lines to remember

  • Directed nets sample top-down with ease; inferring their hidden causes is hard, because observing an effect makes independent causes compete (explaining away) and exact sums run over 2H settings.
  • Auto-regressive nets use the chain rule, one conditional per variable, so log p(x) is exact. FVSBN makes each conditional a logistic regression; NADE shares one hidden layer and gets all D conditionals in O(DH).
  • Moment matching trains a generator by making the kernel mean of its samples equal that of the data; a Gaussian kernel compares every moment, but its bandwidth decides what the generator can see.
  • A denoising autoencoder run as corrupt–denoise–repeat is a Markov chain whose long-run distribution estimates the data; clamping gives conditional samples, walk-back trains away spurious modes, and GSNs learn the transition operator directly.
  • Compare generative models on identical data with like-for-like numbers (exact vs bound vs estimate, nats vs bits per pixel), and never by samples alone: memorising looks perfect and 99% noise costs under 5 nats.

Check your understanding

Why is sampling from a sigmoid belief net easy but computing p(v) hard?

Sampling goes in the direction of the arrows: draw the top layer from its prior, then each layer given its parents, each a simple coin flip. p(v) goes against them: it needs the sum over every hidden configuration, 2H terms, and the posterior does not factorise because observed effects couple their causes (explaining away).

An FVSBN and a NADE both give exact log-likelihoods. What does NADE buy?

Expressiveness and cost. FVSBN’s conditionals are linear in the earlier pixels and need D(D − 1)/2 weights; NADE’s conditionals are non-linear (a hidden layer) yet, because the input weights are shared, all D hidden layers come from one running sum in O(DH) time with D(2H + 1) + H parameters.

Your GMMN uses a Gaussian kernel with a tiny bandwidth and training stalls. Why?

With a tiny bandwidth, k(x, y) is essentially zero unless a sample sits right on a data point, so the witness function is flat almost everywhere and samples far from the data get no gradient. A wider bandwidth (or a mix of bandwidths) gives every sample a slope to follow.

What does it take for a denoising autoencoder’s chain to sample the data distribution?

The denoiser must be (a consistent estimate of) the true conditional P(x | x̃), and the chain must be ergodic: the corruption must let it reach every state. Then the data distribution is its unique stationary distribution. A denoiser with too simple an output distribution, or a corruption too narrow to cross gaps, breaks this.

A paper reports a VAE’s −ELBO of 95 nats against a NADE’s 88 nats. Can you conclude that NADE is the better density model?

Not by itself. −ELBO is an upper bound on the VAE’s true −log p, which may be several nats lower; compare against an importance-weighted or AIS estimate. Also check both used the same binarisation and test set: thresholded and randomly binarised MNIST give quite different numbers.
